newsitem.title: UK: Railtrack says hopes to prove critics wrong. [CORRECTED 13:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Railtrack says hopes to prove critics wrong. [CORRECTED 13:35 GMT]

text.p: Railtrack Plc said on Friday it wanted to prove to its critics -- led by the opposition Labour Party -- that it could operate Britain's railways more effectively now it has been privatised.
Labour has said if it wins the next general election it will use the powers of the rail regulator to make Railtrack spend more on new track and signalling.
It has also threatened to levy a windfall tax on an as yet unspecified number of former state-owned utilities which it says were sold off too cheaply by the Conservative government.

"Railtrack's position is that we want to deliver to our customers in a satisfactory way and then, we feel, the regulator and the politicians will understand our role and not seek to interfere with a successful company," chief executive John Edmonds told a telephone news conference.

He added: "If the Labour Party has the objectives they state, which are higher levels of investmeent and a better quality of service, I hope they will look at what we are actively achieving and conclude that Railtrack is the sort of company they can live comfortably with."

Headline pretax profits for the six months to September 30 jumped to 173 million pounds from 98 million pounds a year ago, boosted by a drop in interest charges of 43 million pounds because the government cut its debt burden before privatisation.
Operating profits rose to 169 million pounds from 151 million a year ago and the company declared its first dividend of 7.3 pence a share.

Finance director Norman Broadhurst said that operating costs rose to 1,035 million pounds from 988 million a year ago but the increase was due to a rephasing of costs to even them out over the full year, as well as the fact that the company paid its maintenance contractors higher bonuses for improved performance.

"Overall if you take away the phasing and the performance bonuses our costs are roughly in line with those of last year which means we have offset the effect of inflation by about three percent," he told the news conference.

Railtrack said in the last six months it had improved the reliability and punctuality of train services while its spending on investment in infrastructure rose 35 percent to 409 million pounds compared to the same period a year ago.
(Company corrects statement on infrastructure investment from "... rose 25 percent to 500 million pounds")

"With the restructuring of the industry and our flotation behind us, we shall devote significant management resources to accelerating our total investment programme," chairman Robert Horton said in a statement.

He said he expected that by the year 2001 Railtrack would have spent eight billion pounds of the total 10 billion pounds it had originally pledged to invest between 1994 and the year 2004 when it took over the national railways.
